title: Scope & Closures
description: Lexical scope, hoisting, TDZ, closures and modules

questions.explanation: The inner block declares its own x that shadows the outer one only inside the braces. After the block ends, x refers to the outer variable again.
Function declarations are hoisted together with their body, so the function can be called before the line it is written on.
The var declaration is hoisted to the top of the function/global scope and initialized to undefined; the assignment = 5 only happens when that line runs.

let and const declarations are hoisted too, but they stay uninitialized until their declaration line runs. Accessing them earlier — the temporal dead zone (TDZ) — throws a ReferenceError ("Cannot access 'v' before initialization").
The inner let x shadows the outer x for the whole block, starting at the opening brace, not at the let line. So console.log(x) refers to the inner x while it is still in its TDZ and throws.
With let in a for loop header, each iteration gets a fresh binding of i, and each callback closes over its own copy. (With var there is a single shared i and you would get 3 3 3.)

questions.prompt: Which description of a closure is most accurate?
options: A copy of a variable's value taken when a function is created
A function's live link to the variables of the scope where it was defined, which persists even after that scope has finished
A function that cannot be called again
A private variable created by the class keyword
questions.explanation: Closure keeps access to the variables themselves, not snapshots. If the variable changes later, the function sees the new value.
Closures capture variables, not values. show reads n when it is called, and by then n has been updated to 2.

This is the module pattern: count lives in the factory's scope and can only be reached through the public methods that close over it. counter.count is undefined because count was never a property of the returned object.

questions.prompt: Which statement about ES modules (import/export) is true?
options: Every file shares a single global scope
Each module has its own top-level scope, runs in strict mode, and only exported bindings are visible to importers
Modules are re-executed every time they are imported
Variables in modules are automatically added to window
questions.explanation: Top-level declarations in a module are local to that module. Modules are always strict, are evaluated once (later imports get the same instance) and expose only what they export.

questions.prompt: What does this log in a browser script that is NOT a module?
questions.explanation: In a classic (non-module) script, a top-level var becomes a property of the global object (window), but let/const/class are global variables without a matching property. Inside a module neither would appear on window.

questions.prompt: What is an IIFE mainly used for?
options: Creating a new scope immediately so its variables don't leak into the surrounding scope
Delaying a function until the page loads
questions.explanation: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression — (function () { … })() — runs once right away and keeps its inner variables private. In modern code a plain block with let/const or an ES module often achieves the same.
